items.questionAndWhy: How does repeated experience transform a newly learned motor response into a durable skill? The distinction matters because rapid short-term adaptation may not predict later, independent performance.
items.whatTheyDid: Franklin, Nietschmann and Franklin studied healthy young adults adapting reaching movements to an unfamiliar velocity-dependent force field. Ten participants completed an exploratory protocol and eighteen took part in a preregistered extension. Eight training sessions provided repeated practice, followed by retention and generalization tests across approximately fifteen weeks.
items.whatTheyFound: With extensive practice, compensation approached 95% of the imposed dynamics, retention and spontaneous recovery strengthened, and learned responses became more narrowly tuned to trained movement directions. These are controlled sensorimotor outcomes in a small adult sample, not evidence that every cognitive or social skill consolidates similarly.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX practitioner courses could distinguish immediate task success from delayed retention and generalization. A concrete experiment would compare repeated scenario practice with one-off instruction, using later unaided performance as the outcome. Transfer from motor adaptation to analytical skill acquisition is a hypothesis, not a finding of this study.
items.streamTitle: Long-term motor learning became more stable and specialized over fifteen weeks
items.streamSummary: Repeated force-field reaching practice in 28 adults produced stronger retention and more specialized responses over weeks. It supports testing delayed skill retention, not assuming cognitive-training transfer.
items.attribution: Franklin, Nietschmann and Franklin — Nature Human Behaviour (motor-learning experiments, November 9)

items.questionAndWhy: When do AI platform features and peer recommendations relate to trust and intended purchases? The behavioral question is whether apparent transparency always builds trust, or whether privacy concerns change that relationship.
items.whatTheyDid: Ma and Zheng surveyed 979 Generation Z university students in China about AI-system transparency, usability, online word of mouth, personal trust propensity, privacy concern, information gathering, consumer trust and purchase intentions. They fitted an extended stimulus–organism–response model with mediation and moderation paths.
items.whatTheyFound: Reported transparency, user-friendliness and online word of mouth were associated with trust and purchase intentions. Privacy concerns weakened the transparency–trust association; information gathering strengthened the word-of-mouth–trust association. Self-reported cross-sectional data cannot demonstrate that platform features caused trust or that stated intentions became actual purchases.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX, platform design, privacy expectations and perceived peer opinion are separable candidate predictors of information-source trust. An experimentally manipulated interface or recommendation study could evaluate these relations; the Chinese student survey alone does not establish causal influence or generalize to political audiences.
items.streamTitle: Privacy concerns conditioned Gen Z trust in AI-mediated commerce
items.streamSummary: A 979-student Chinese survey linked AI transparency, peer recommendations and usability to trust and purchase intention, with privacy-related moderation. All pathways are observational.
items.attribution: Ma and Zheng — Scientific Reports (cross-sectional Gen Z consumer survey, November 10)

items.questionAndWhy: Do professionals respond more cautiously when organizations emphasize AI in their public disclosures? The study asks whether institutional signaling is associated with changes in observed audit procedures.
items.whatTheyDid: Huang examined 31,389 firm-year observations from Chinese A-share companies across 2016–2024. The archival analysis related AI-related wording in corporate disclosures to audit-report delays and fees, with comparisons around regulatory developments, auditor type and firm characteristics.
items.whatTheyFound: More intensive AI-related disclosure was associated with longer audit delays, interpreted cautiously as an indicator of audit prudence. The relationship varied after regulatory changes and with Big Four auditors; some proposed moderators, including state ownership and AI-sector status, were not significant. Disclosure density and audit delay are proxies; firm-level observational associations do not isolate auditors' psychology or establish causal effects.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX organizational sensemaking, this suggests a testable question about how novel-technology claims alter perceived uncertainty and verification choices. Direct experiments with professional decision-makers would be required before claiming that AI rhetoric itself causes caution.
items.streamTitle: Corporate AI rhetoric correlated with longer audit delays, with institutional differences
items.streamSummary: An archival study of 31,389 Chinese firm-years linked AI-focused disclosure to longer audit delays; some auditor and regulatory contexts moderated the association. It is not causal evidence of individual auditor cognition.
items.attribution: Huang — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (firm-level archival study, November 10)

items.questionAndWhy: What features of civilian resilience under crisis and war should security planners actually assess? Capability planning requires separating observed adaptation from broad claims that a population is resilient.
items.whatTheyDid: Lindgren and colleagues prepared a 48-page NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence limited literature review, published October 9, examining civilian responses to disruptive crises and war with particular attention to Northern European allied settings. They considered resilience concepts, relevant contextual factors and implications for assessment.
items.whatTheyFound: The review identifies a need to examine how people and institutions cope with disruption, including differences between formal preparedness and enacted adaptation. It compiles prior evidence and assessment considerations rather than conducting a new field experiment or validating one intervention's effectiveness. Geographic and evidence-base limitations constrain transfer.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX operations research, a resilience assessment could distinguish household and organizational resources, perceived support, adaptation decisions and continuity of essential behavior. This is a proposed measurement agenda, not a demonstrated effect of strategic communication or resilience training.
items.streamTitle: NATO resilience review distinguished civilian adaptation from untested interventions
items.streamSummary: A 48-page NATO StratCom literature review identifies civilian adaptation and assessment considerations for crises and war. It supplies practitioner questions rather than validated effects of any single resilience intervention.
items.attribution: Lindgren, Svenonius, Palmer and Bertolin — NATO StratCom COE (limited literature review, October 9)

items.questionAndWhy: When is it appropriate to disrupt an actor conducting foreign information manipulation instead of only rebutting individual claims? The operational choice requires evidence about actors, tactics, context and potential costs.
items.whatTheyDid: Colley's 44-page NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence report reviewed counter-FIMI practice and research, with a focus on measures intended to interrupt hostile actors or operations. It compared possible responses and discussed assessment and coordination requirements.
items.whatTheyFound: The author argues that fact-checking and media literacy alone do not exhaust the response options and that context-specific disruption should be considered. The review also notes substantial evidence gaps: a recommendation or reported activity is not a measured reduction in manipulation, reach or behavior. The report does not constitute a randomized test of disruption strategies.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX, counter-FIMI COAs should have explicit mechanisms, potential side effects, thresholds for attribution, and separate activity, disruption and audience-outcome measures. Using the report as an options framework is source-supported; asserting that any recommended tactic works generally would exceed the evidence.
items.streamTitle: Counter-FIMI review argued for disruption while acknowledging thin effectiveness evidence
items.streamSummary: A NATO StratCom review considers disrupting hostile information actors beyond fact-checking, while noting limited comparative evidence of effectiveness. It offers COA assessment questions, not established operational effects.
items.attribution: Thomas Colley — NATO StratCom COE (counter-FIMI analytical report, July 31)

items.questionAndWhy: Can automated AI judges reliably assess whether replies to online hate are coherent, relevant, nonaggressive and suitable? Scaling evaluation without agreement with human experts risks misranking interventions.
items.whatTheyDid: Alali, Ocampo and Ceolin evaluated twelve open-weight language models against expert-labeled CSEval counterspeech examples. They tested pointwise and pairwise judgments under different prompting conditions, then computed agreement and rank correlations for four quality dimensions.
items.whatTheyFound: The best reported pointwise configuration had linear-weighted Cohen's kappa 0.19 and Spearman rho 0.42; a direct pairwise comparison reached kappa 0.25. Converting pointwise ratings into pairwise decisions raised kappa to 0.35 in one setting. Some models agreed strongly with one another (kappa 0.76) while remaining weakly aligned with experts (at most 0.21 in the reported comparison). These are label-agreement tests, not observed hate reduction.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX, model consensus should not substitute for human-validated judgments of message quality. If AI judges are used to screen response alternatives, report criterion-specific human agreement and test downstream behavior separately. This evidence does not show whether counterspeech actually changes audience behavior.
items.streamTitle: LLM judges agreed with each other more than with human counterspeech experts
items.streamSummary: Twelve open LLMs showed low agreement with human experts when rating counterspeech, even where model-to-model agreement was strong. Automatic scoring needs human benchmarking and is not evidence of intervention effectiveness.
items.attribution: Alali, Ocampo and Ceolin — arXiv preprint (counterspeech-judge evaluation, November 3)

items.questionAndWhy: Can AI agents learn from earlier human corrections at the specific decision point where they matter, rather than merely retrieving a past conversation? This targets repeated mistakes in long research workflows.
items.whatTheyDid: Vahdat and Vaezipoor described Decision Context, a system converting corrections and tool failures into scoped procedural rules for future agent actions. They evaluated it on DC-Bench, 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, using deterministic mock tool results based on executed traces.
items.whatTheyFound: The proposed rule-based approach achieved approximately 95% conditional compliance, compared with roughly 55% for a naive retrieval baseline, while using substantially fewer injected context tokens. These are controlled benchmark results with mocked outputs, not a field test demonstrating reliable scientific work or independence from oversight.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX agents could test whether documented failure-specific rules reduce repeated provenance, file-handling or process errors. Replays should verify actual final artifacts and guard against brittle or conflicting rules. Improved benchmark compliance does not demonstrate improved human modeling or scientific validity.
items.streamTitle: Persistent agent correction rules improved compliance in a controlled benchmark
items.streamSummary: Decision Context converted agent corrections into scoped rules and reported about 95% benchmark compliance versus 55% for naive retrieval. Mocked tool traces limit claims about deployed research reliability.
items.attribution: Vahdat and Vaezipoor — arXiv preprint (agent-memory benchmark, November 5)

items.questionAndWhy: Can existing English-language NLP measures of episodic autobiographical narrative detail be reused for another language through translation without materially degrading measurement?
items.whatTheyDid: Groer and colleagues tested an automatic internal-versus-external detail-scoring workflow using 1,920 German autobiographical narratives from 258 people. They translated narratives to English, applied an existing English-language model and compared output with human annotations and alternative processing choices.
items.whatTheyFound: The translated workflow showed strong correspondence with manually scored details and little reported degradation relative to the tested alternatives. Results concern the sampled German narratives and this scoring construct; human annotations are an imperfect benchmark, and performance in other languages, clinical populations or intelligence interviews is untested.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX cross-cultural narrative research, translation plus structured coding could be piloted against bilingual human adjudication rather than assuming every language needs a separately trained model. Separate measurement invariance from usefulness for operational interpretation; translation fidelity is not proof of identical cultural meaning.
items.streamTitle: Translation-enabled scoring extracted autobiographical detail from German narratives
items.streamSummary: A study of 1,920 German autobiographical narratives found translation-to-English enabled automated internal/external detail scoring with little observed degradation against manual ratings. Cross-cultural field transfer needs validation.
items.attribution: Groer, Külpmann, Zlomuzica and Plank — Scientific Reports (multilingual narrative measurement, November 10)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a fitted dynamical model produce dependable intervention counterfactuals when small uncertainty in starting conditions, parameters or noise grows over time? This matters for model-based course-of-action comparisons.
items.whatTheyDid: Aalaila, Großmann, Mukherjee and colleagues examined structural causal representations of dynamical systems, including Lorenz and Rössler chaotic systems and a nonchaotic logistic growth comparison. They used simulated observations, state-space inference and nested particle filtering to estimate parameters and examine counterfactual trajectories after interventions.
items.whatTheyFound: In chaotic regimes, seemingly small uncertainties could produce dramatically diverging later counterfactual trajectories, even where the model described observed dynamics well; nonchaotic settings were comparatively more stable. These are mathematical and synthetic-system findings, not evidence that any given human influence process is chaotic.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX COA simulation, a high fit to historical trajectories is insufficient for long-horizon intervention confidence. Compare forecast horizons, structural and initial-state uncertainty, and robustness across plausible assumptions. Applying chaotic-system conclusions to social dynamics is a methodological hypothesis requiring empirical tests.
items.streamTitle: Chaotic systems exposed fragility of long-horizon counterfactual predictions
items.streamSummary: Formal counterfactual simulations showed that small uncertainties can amplify dramatically in chaotic dynamics despite adequate factual fit. This cautions long-horizon COA modeling; human-system applicability is untested.
items.attribution: Aalaila, Großmann, Mukherjee et al. — Scientific Reports (formal counterfactual simulation study, June 2)

items.questionAndWhy: Can researchers combine time-aligned task behavior and portable brain measurements to evaluate changes in attention around an immersive activity? Reproducible instrumentation matters before claims about training effectiveness.
items.whatTheyDid: Li and Yang released a Scientific Data dataset from 42 healthy young adults randomized to VR-integrated cycling, ordinary cycling or a no-intervention control. The package contains pre/post Stroop-task behavior, prefrontal functional near-infrared spectroscopy, heart-rate information, event markers, demographics and analysis resources.
items.whatTheyFound: The publication's primary deliverable is a documented, reusable multimodal dataset and processing pipeline. The design permits comparisons among the three conditions, but the Data Descriptor does not independently establish that immersive cycling improves sustained attention, training retention or real-world operational performance. Sample size and participant population limit generalization.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX XR research, the concrete technology contribution is synchronized behavioral, physiological and task-event recording with shared analysis resources. This can inform measurement design for cognitive load or attention studies; transferring to practitioner training or influence assessment remains untested.
items.streamTitle: Open Stroop, fNIRS and VR-cycling dataset enabled linked attention measurements
items.streamSummary: A November 11 Scientific Data release provides synchronized Stroop, fNIRS and physiological records from 42 randomized young adults around VR versus ordinary cycling and control. It is an enabling dataset, not proven XR training efficacy.
items.attribution: Li and Yang — Scientific Data (open multimodal XR/attention dataset, November 11)
